basic_identification.name: Residency/grant infrastructure for digital artists
basic_identification.originator: Systemic gap across arts funding ecosystem. Partial responses from Villa Albertine, SETI Institute, Harvestworks, EMAP, Creative Capital, NEW INC, Max Planck Institute
basic_identification.year: Ongoing deficit recognized since mid-2010s, acute since 2022 post-NFT crash
basic_identification.geography: Global gap. Existing programs concentrated in North America and Western Europe. Near-zero infrastructure in Global South, Southeast Asia, Africa, Latin America

core_ideas.core_claim: Funding mechanisms for digital artists lag behind the pace of practice. Few residencies are designed specifically for code-based, generative, or AI-based artistic work. Most grant programs still orient around traditional media categories, and digital artists must retrofit their practice into frameworks designed for painting, sculpture, or film.
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Code-based and AI-based art requires compute resources, server access, GPU time, software licenses, and iterative technical development cycles that traditional residency models do not accommodate. A painter needs studio space; a generative artist needs cloud compute credits and blockchain deployment budgets. Most residencies provide the former, not the latter.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: Grant infrastructure currently rewards attention-legible practices. Artists with large social media followings or viral NFT sales history find it easier to secure support. Residencies that evaluate work through traditional portfolio review often cannot assess generative or interactive work adequately. The gap reinforces attention-driven selection by default, not by design.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: This is an intention-aligned gap. The field structurally needs sustainable funding for practitioners whose work does not generate market returns. Without dedicated infrastructure, only market-successful digital artists survive, which collapses the field's diversity. Addressing this gap serves declared structural needs rather than engagement capture.

market_economics.revenue_model: Grants are funded through foundations (Mellon, Ford, Kresge), government agencies (NEA, Arts Council England, Creative Europe), corporate sponsorship (OpenAI residency, tech company partnerships), and endowments. Few programs are self-sustaining. Most depend on philanthropic cycles.
market_economics.market_position: Infrastructure — sits outside the value chain of art sales. Enables practice that may later enter primary or secondary markets but does not participate in transactions directly.
market_economics.price_range: Grant amounts range from EUR 4,000 (EMAP) to USD 50,000 (Creative Capital, Pollock-Krasner). Typical digital-specific residency stipends: USD 2,000-5,000 (Harvestworks), USD 30,000 over two years (SETI). Most programs also cover accommodation, travel, and production costs.
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Slowly growing. New programs launched 2024-2025 include Villa Albertine AI residency, SETI Algorithmic Imaginings, Max Planck Artist & AI. But growth is from a very low base. The NFT crash reduced corporate and crypto-funded residencies significantly. Overall trajectory: cautious expansion with institutional backing replacing crypto-era sponsorship.
market_economics.collector_demographics: Not applicable — grants and residencies do not involve collectors. However, the absence of grant infrastructure pushes artists toward collector-dependent models, skewing the field toward market-friendly work.
market_economics.sustainability: Most programs depend on grant cycles and philanthropic funding, which are themselves cyclical. Few residencies have endowments. The sustainability gap is recursive: the infrastructure meant to sustain artists is itself unsustainable. Programs like Creative Capital (founded 1999, still active) demonstrate that longevity is possible with diversified funding, but most digital-specific programs are too young to have proven durability.

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Residencies for digital artists require provision of: compute infrastructure (GPU access, cloud credits), software licenses, blockchain deployment budgets, display technology (screens, projectors, LED walls), sensor/hardware kits for interactive work, and technical mentorship. Most existing programs provide only studio space and a stipend.
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: AI-specific residencies are the fastest-growing segment (Villa Albertine, SETI, Max Planck, OpenAI). However, these tend to frame AI as subject matter for critical inquiry rather than as a creative medium. Few programs support artists who use AI as a core production tool without requiring critical-distance framing.
practice_aesthetics.liveness: Not applicable to infrastructure itself, but the gap particularly affects artists working in real-time, generative, and interactive modes, which require sustained technical development time that short-term residencies cannot support.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: The vocabulary for evaluating code-based and AI-based work in grant applications is still forming. Review panels often lack technical literacy to assess generative systems, interactive installations, or on-chain works. Terms like 'creative coding,' 'generative art,' and 'AI art' are used loosely and inconsistently across applications and evaluation criteria.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: Openness over enclosure (grants are non-extractive). Commons over capture (residencies generate shared knowledge). Infrastructure over spectacle (funding enables practice, not display). Individual focus but collective benefit (supporting individual artists strengthens the field).

infrastructure_governance.openness: Mixed. Government-funded programs (NEA, Creative Europe) are typically open-call with transparent criteria. Foundation-funded programs vary. Corporate residencies (OpenAI) are often invitation-only or highly selective with opaque criteria.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: Typically expert-committee or curatorial. Selection panels often comprise curators, past awardees, and arts administrators. Few programs include technologists or practicing digital artists on review panels, creating a structural bias toward traditional-art-legible proposals.
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Artists typically retain full IP rights to work produced during residencies. However, some corporate-sponsored programs (especially AI company residencies) may include clauses about use of outputs for promotional purposes. Grant agreements vary but generally favor artist ownership.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Low. No standardized application format across programs. No shared database of digital art residencies. Artists must discover opportunities through fragmented channels (social media, email lists, ResArtis, TransArtists). No API or structured data layer connecting programs.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: Absent at the infrastructure level. Residency programs rarely address preservation of works produced. Artworks created during residencies may be exhibited temporarily but often lack long-term preservation plans. This compounds the archival gap for born-digital works.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Varies by program. Application processes collect artist data with varying privacy standards. Some programs share applicant information with partners without explicit consent. Machine-readable consent frameworks are absent across the sector.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: Parallel and subordinate. Traditional residency programs (Skowhegan, MacDowell, Yaddo) occasionally accept digital artists but do not provide digital-specific infrastructure. Dedicated digital programs exist outside the prestige hierarchy of established residencies.
field_position.what_it_enables: When functional, residency/grant infrastructure enables: sustained research and development time free from market pressure, cross-pollination between practitioners, technical experimentation without commercial viability requirements, and career development for emerging artists who cannot self-fund practice.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Dedicated compute and technical infrastructure. Review panels with digital art literacy. Funding for ongoing maintenance of generative/interactive works after residency ends. Programs specifically for Global South digital artists. Mid-career support (most programs target emerging artists). Mechanisms to fund collaborative or collective practice rather than individual artists only.
field_position.who_is_excluded: Artists in the Global South (few programs, high travel costs, visa barriers). Self-taught coders without MFA credentials (many programs require formal art education). Artists working in emerging or non-legible media (custom software, blockchain-native work, AI systems). Non-English speakers (most applications require English). Artists without institutional affiliation.
field_position.frontier_signal: Emerging. The gap is widely recognized but solutions are fragmented. New AI-focused residencies represent frontier activity. The field is transitioning from crypto-funded models to institutional and philanthropic models.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: Word of mouth, social media, mailing lists (e.g., Rhizome, CreativeApplications.net), ResArtis database, TransArtists. No centralized discovery platform for digital art-specific opportunities. Information asymmetry is high.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: Moderate. Artists with social media visibility and institutional connections learn about opportunities first. However, the application process itself is not attention-driven — it rewards proposal quality over follower count. The gap is in discovery, not selection.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Strongly intention-aligned when it exists. Grants and residencies serve declared structural needs: sustaining practice, enabling experimentation, building careers. The gap itself represents a failure of intention — the field knows it needs this infrastructure but has not built it at scale.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: Potentially high but currently unrealized. Residencies could contribute to shared field knowledge if they required open documentation, published research outcomes, or contributed to shared resources. Most programs do not have such requirements, so knowledge generated during residencies remains individual.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Neither. Grant and residency infrastructure does not track provenance of any kind. Works produced during residencies have no standardized provenance documentation linking them to the context of their creation.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Cyclical — tied to annual grant cycles, application deadlines, and funding periods. This creates boom-bust dynamics for artists who depend on sequential residencies.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: This item IS an absence. It represents what is missing from the field's infrastructure. The gap itself is poorly documented — no comprehensive audit of digital art funding exists. Most analysis focuses on what programs exist rather than what is structurally absent.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Neither. The residency/grant landscape is fragmented without coherence or consensus. Each program operates independently with different criteria, values, and definitions of digital art. No shared framework connects them.
coherence.contestability: Low. Grant decisions are typically final and non-appealable. Rejection reasons are rarely disclosed. Artists cannot contest or understand selection criteria in most programs. This opacity particularly disadvantages artists working in unfamiliar media.
coherence.forkability: High in principle — anyone can create a new residency program. Low in practice — funding, institutional support, and administrative infrastructure create significant barriers. Community-organized alternatives (artist-run residencies, DAO-funded programs) represent partial forks.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: A(DAI) should learn from the discovery gap here: build a structured, searchable layer of funding opportunities as part of its field intelligence. Map existing programs, track deadlines, document selection criteria, and identify geographic and medium-specific gaps. This would be a high-value commons contribution. A(DAI) should also adopt the principle that sustainable practice requires non-market funding mechanisms.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: A(DAI) should refuse to replicate the individual-artist-genius model that most grant programs assume. Funding infrastructure should also support collectives, scenes, and infrastructure builders, not only individual art production. A(DAI) should also refuse the geographic centrism of existing programs.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: A(DAI) is a collective intelligence infrastructure; most grant programs are designed for individual artists. The tension is between collective field-building and individual career support. A(DAI) can bridge this by making the grant landscape itself legible and navigable — turning individual knowledge about opportunities into shared field intelligence.

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: Grant programs must comply with arts funding regulations in their jurisdictions. EU programs (Creative Europe, EMAP) follow EU cultural policy frameworks. US programs navigate NEA funding restrictions and nonprofit compliance. Tax treatment of grants varies by country. No specific AI Act or digital-specific regulation applies to grant-making itself, though AI residencies may produce work that falls under EU AI Act transparency requirements.
regulatory_legal.ip_model: Typically artist-retains-all-rights. Some corporate residencies include promotional use clauses. Government-funded programs may require public access to outputs. No standardized IP framework across the sector.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Opt-in by design — artists choose to apply. However, the discovery gap means many eligible artists never learn about opportunities, creating a de facto exclusion that is neither opt-in nor opt-out but structural invisibility.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: Low platform dependency for the infrastructure itself. However, the discovery of opportunities depends heavily on social media platforms (Instagram, Twitter/X) and email newsletter services. If these platforms change algorithms or policies, opportunity discovery is affected.
ecosystem.network_effects: Weak positive network effects. Residency alumni networks create some compounding value (past residents recommend programs, mentor future cohorts). But these networks are fragmented and informal. No structured network connects digital art residency alumni across programs.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: Post-2022 crash: crypto-funded residencies (DAO-sponsored, NFT platform-funded) largely disappeared. Institutional and philanthropic programs survived and are slowly expanding. New AI-focused programs emerging. Overall: pivoting from crypto-era models to traditional arts funding models with digital-specific adaptations. Growing but from a very low base.
